# What makes a good 'data story'?

::: {.notes}
Not every story needs data to be told. Numbers and charts are tools for communicating information, just like paragraphs and images are, and it's important to consider how and when to deploy them in a way that's meaningful and engaging.
:::

## First, start with:

[A question or a problem]{.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="1"}

[A gap in knowledge or information]{.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="2"}

[An observation]{.fragment .fade-in data-fragment-index="3"}

::: {.notes}
Question: Why is this happening? What's causing it? How long has this been happening?

Gap: Nobody has looked at it at this angle before

Observation: Very interesting, because often it comes from you and what you notice
:::

---

![](images/vogue1.png){style="max-width: 500px; display: block; margin: 0 auto; margin-bottom: 20px;"}
![](images/vogue2.png){style="max-width: 500px; display: block; margin: 0 auto;"}

::: {.notes}
This author noticed that recent Vogue covers have less text than they did a decade ago. They looked at every Vogue cover and measured how much physical space the text on the covers took up.
:::

:::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/strava.jpg)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/strava2.jpg)
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Strava heatmap of Baltimore. These brighter lines indicate higher activity -- more runners there. Noticed that this maps to the 'white L', predominantly white, wealthy area in Baltimore, while the surrounding darker areas are Black neighborhoods.

Just these two maps tell an entire story.

Sometimes all it takes is taking a closer look at a thing or environment you already know.
:::

## Then consider:

[Is this story interesting or worth telling?]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Does the data exist? If not, can I collect it?]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Is data viz the right medium to convey this information?]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Who is my audience?]{.fragment .fade-in}

::: {.notes}
So whenever I approach a new story, I go through this mental checklist:

- Either for you, for your organization, or for other people. What's driving you to tell this story?
- This is a question I imagine all of you have asked yourselves. Often this is where we have to pivot
- This entirely depends on the story. Sometimes eyewitness accounts, case studies, photographs can go a longer way
- More technical, less technical? Put yourself in their shoes -- without context other than what they're looking at, how might they interpret it?
:::

::: {.notes}
Maps/cartography


NYT: literal heatmap of neighborhoods in Richmond, VA. They measured shade coverage and heat in different neighborhoods and compared this map to old redline maps.

Redlining is a practice where neighborhoods would be graded based on their desirability and risk -- often as a discriminatory practice against Black neighborhoods. Banks and companies could use this to deny loans and services to these areas.

Overlap.
:::

# 3. Designing good data viz

---

[Communicate information clearly and concisely]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Be conscious of cognitive load]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Have a point of view]{.fragment .fade-in}

[Be delightful]{.fragment .fade-in}

::: {.notes}
Cognitive load: how much effort it takes to understand the information? design systems, ease of interaction and interpretability
:::

# 3. Designing <span style="font-style: italic; color: var(--color-green);">great</span> data viz
